children: Brazil's federal tax authority cut its revenue forecast by nearly two-thirds for a dividend tax introduced this year, underscoring weaker-than-expected collections from a measure that had been expected to provide a significant boost to government coffers.

The new estimate is around 10 billion reais ($1.95 billion), down from an initial forecast of roughly 29 billion reais, Claudemir Malaquias, head of the tax revenue service's Center for Tax and Customs Studies, told reporters on Tuesday.
Collections from the tax have totaled 4.3 billion reais from January to August, he added.

According to Malaquias, the revised figures will be formally released later this week when President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's government publishes its next bimonthly report on projected revenues and expenditures for the year.
Malaquias said dividend tax collections had fallen short of expectations, but added that higher-than-expected revenue from other sources would partly offset the shortfall, without providing details.
Reuters reported in April that Brazil's new dividend tax had raised only a fraction of the revenue initially expected this year, according to previously undisclosed tax data.

The weak performance started raising questions about whether the measure would generate enough revenue to fund Lula's flagship expansion of income tax exemptions for Brazilians earning up to 5,000 reais ($976.35) per month, which began this year.

Under measures introduced this year, the government started levying a 10% withholding tax on dividend payments above 50,000 reais made by companies to individuals, as well as on all dividend remittances abroad to provide due fiscal compensation.
The government's economic team had for months argued that the plan to broaden income tax exemptions would be fiscally neutral.
